## Week 7: tuning and regularization

Every method so far had a knob. This week: choosing it by $K$-fold cross-validation, with the curve it draws against $\lambda$, $k$ and tree depth, and the standard error of a held-out score. Then how the error depends on $n$ and the number of inputs: from the bias--variance decomposition, the error of $k$-nearest neighbors with $p$ inputs, the rate $n^{-2/(p+2)}$, and the faster rates an additive or a sparse truth allows. Ridge and the lasso side by side in the simplest design: shrinkage against soft thresholding, and selection against prediction; the smoothing penalty on a spline as ridge with weights. Double descent: which zero-error fit you get past the interpolation threshold, why the test error can fall again, and why that does not contradict the bias--variance trade-off.

**Reading**

- ISLR Chapter 5 (Resampling Methods), section 5.1, pp. 198–208: the validation set, leave-one-out and $K$-fold cross-validation, and the bias--variance trade-off in choosing $K$. Skim 5.1.5 (classification), pp. 206–208. Section 5.2, the bootstrap, is not needed this week.
- ISLR Chapter 6, section 6.2.3, pp. 250–251 (choosing the tuning parameter by cross-validation), picking up where the last reading stopped. Re-read "A simple special case for ridge regression and the lasso", pp. 247–249: the lecture works in that design.
- ISLR Chapter 6, section 6.4, pp. 261–267 (what changes when $p > n$). Section 6.3, which comes between them, is not part of the course.
- ISLR Chapter 7, section 7.5.1, pp. 301–302 (smoothing splines: a penalty on wiggliness instead of a basis size). Skim 7.5.2, pp. 302–304.

Optional: PPA Chapter 6 (Generalization), "Generalization gap" and "Overparameterization: empirical phenomena", pp. 100–104 (the double-descent curve, and why it is not universal); ISLR section 10.8, pp. 439–443 (interpolation and double descent, with the natural-spline example the lecture demonstrates); ISLR section 3.5, pp. 105–110, re-read (what happens to $k$-nearest neighbors as the number of inputs grows).

Deeper: ESL section 7.10.2, pp. 245–247 (the wrong and the right way to do cross-validation, which the seminar meets); ESL section 2.5, pp. 22–28 (local methods in high dimensions); ESL sections 3.4.1–3.4.3, pp. 61–73 (ridge and the lasso in general designs); Belkin, M., Hsu, D., Ma, S. and Mandal, S. (2019), "Reconciling modern machine-learning practice and the classical bias--variance trade-off", *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* 116(32), 15849--15854, [doi:10.1073/pnas.1903070116](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1903070116); Györfi, L., Kohler, M., Krzyżak, A. and Walk, H. (2002), *A Distribution-Free Theory of Nonparametric Regression*, Springer, New York, [doi:10.1007/b97848](https://doi.org/10.1007/b97848), Chapter 6, and Stone, C. J. (1982), "Optimal global rates of convergence for nonparametric regression", *Annals of Statistics* 10(4), 1040--1053, [doi:10.1214/aos/1176345969](https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176345969), for the rigorous and the minimax form of the nearest-neighbor rate the lecture derives from a stated lemma.
